paper_title: Length Is Cheap, Competition Is Not: Attention Predicts Context Rot in Retrieval

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Why do language models fail on long inputs? The common answer is length. We show that, for retrieval, length is cheap and competition is not. On five open models (0.5B to 3B parameters, four families), neutral filler costs nothing: accuracy stays at 0.97 to 1.00, up to 32K tokens on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Statements in the format of the evidence, placed at the same positions, drop it to 0.16 to 0.33. A single statement that gives the queried key a rival value multiplies the loss by 9 to 110, and every additional rival adds to it. Inside the model, one quantity tracks the failure: the attention mass left on the evidence. Across 126,473 trials it explains up to 58% of the variance in loss; log length explains at most 8%. The masked-filler protocol behind the claim that length alone hurts reproduces on MMLU (11 to 18 points lost at 30K tokens), but fails a visible control in retrieval: masking costs 45 accuracy points at 32K tokens, while the same filler left visible costs none. In retrieval, context rot is a competition for attention. We release the probe and all 126K trial-level measurements.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Thirty-two thousand tokens of neutral text cost 1.5B-parameter model nothing. few sentences that contradict the evidence cost it most of its accuracy. This paper is about the gap between those two facts. Language models now accept hundreds of thousands of tokens [17], yet they use far fewer [810]. Retrieval accuracy declines as inputs grow [8, 1115], degradation now called context rot [16, 17]. The prevailing explanation is length itself: Du et al. [18] hid the added tokens from attention, kept their positions, and still measured loss. If length is the cause, the remedy is architectural, and every added token is tax. Length, however, never grows alone. Every added token is also added content, and in realistic inputs much of that content resembles what the model is looking for. Softmax attention [19] makes the distinction consequential. The weight on the evidence is = es es + j= esj , 1 where is the attention score of the evidence and sj the scores of all other keys. thousand dissimilar tokens with low sj add little to the denominator; handful of near-copies of the evidence can halve a. If this is what happens inside the model, context rot is problem of competition, not of size, the remedy is to curate what enters the context, and should predict the loss better than length does. We test this prediction directly. In key-value retrieval task, we vary context length from 512 to 32K tokens, fill the same positions either with neutral material or with statements that share the format of the evidence, and measure on every trial both the log-probability of the correct answer and the attention mass that the model places on the evidence. We study five open models from 0.5B to 3B parameters from four families. Figure 1 summarizes the outcome: at equal length, the loss follows what the context contains and how much attention the evidence keeps, not how many tokens surround it. Our contributions are: 1. Length is cheap; competition is not. With neutral filler, accuracy stays between 0.97 and 1.00 on four of five models, up to 4K tokens on all four and up to 32K on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Filling the same positions with statements in the evidence template drives accuracy to 0.11 to 0.21 at 8K to 32K tokens. The loss concentrates on statements that give the queried key rival value: one such statement multiplies the loss by 9 to 110, and the loss grows with their number at fixed length. 2. Attention mass on the evidence predicts the loss. Across 126,473 trials on five models, log(1/a) explains 35 to 58% of the variance in loss, against 2 to 8% for log length, and the gap persists from 8K to 32K tokens. 3. Masking is not length baseline. Replicating the masked-filler protocol of Du et al. [18], MMLU accuracy falls by 11 to 18 points at 30K masked tokens on Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-7B. In retrieval, the same masking costs 46 points of accuracy at 32K tokens while the identical filler left visible costs none. 4. An open probe. We release the harness, the attention probe, and all trial-level data: code at https://github.com/yliusci/length-is-cheap, data at https://huggingface. co/datasets/yliusci/length-is-cheap.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Long-context degradation. Accuracy falls as inputs grow, well before the nominal context limit [2027]. Liu et al. [11] showed that retrieval depends on where evidence sits [see also 2833]; RULER [8] found effective lengths far below advertised ones; NoLiMa [34] showed that removing lexical overlap between question and evidence accelerates the decline. Hong et al. [16] named the phenomenon context rot across 18 frontier models. These studies vary length and content together, so they cannot say which of the two is responsible. Knowledge conflicts. When context contains statements that disagree, models often follow the wrong one [35; 36; 37; 38; see 39, for survey]. Proactive interference, in which earlier values of key disrupt retrieval of the latest one, drives accuracy log-linearly toward zero as updates accumulate [40]. This literature treats conflicts as reliability problem, separate from length. We show that, in long-context retrieval, rivals carry most of the loss that grows with length. Length or content? Two lines of work give opposite answers. Du et al. [18] masked every distracting token from attention while preserving position indices and still observed drops of at least 7.9% at 30K tokens, concluding that length alone hurts. Conversely, studies that hold length fixed and vary what fills it find that semantically competing material dominates [41, 42]: hard distractors 2 Table 1: Controls in the closest prior work. Study Length fixed, content varied Visible neutral filler Masked filler Attention vs. loss, per trial Du et al. [18] Gao et al. [43] Repantis et al. [44] Hong et al. [16] Ours no yes yes partial yes whitespace repeated text no no three text types yes no no no yes, replicated no head-level margins no no yes, 126K trials collapse accuracy within the first 10% of the context [43], competing passages shorten retention at constant passage count [44; see also 45; 46], and near-miss negatives, not corpus size, bound retrieval at scale [47, 48]. Earlier, Levy et al. [15] and Shi et al. [49] showed that similar padding or single irrelevant sentence suffices to degrade reasoning in short contexts [5052]. Only Gao et al. [43] inspect attention, through logit margins on retrieval heads; none relates the attention on the evidence to the loss trial by trial, so none can tell how much of the failure competitors explain by drawing attention away from the evidence. Attention dilution theory. Softmax attention assigns each key share that shrinks as keys accumulate. Chiang and Cholak [53] and Veličković et al. [54] proved that this dispersion limits sharp retrieval as length grows [5557]; Nakanishi [58] and Chen et al. [59] derived length-dependent temperature corrections [60, 61]; Ghaffari et al. [62] modeled distractors as extreme-value competitors whose maximum score grows with their number, requiring the evidence margin to grow as log . Tworkowski et al. [63] first described this distraction issue: relevant keys become vanishing fraction of all keys, and similar keys compete. These accounts predict that degradation should track the attention mass left on the evidence. That prediction has not been tested trial by trial on measured attention in pretrained models. Our position. We do not claim the phenomenon, the distractor effect, or the dilution theory. We close the loop between them, measuring behavior, content and attention on the evidence in the same trials  (Table 1)  . Du et al. [18] also used visible baseline, but filled it with whitespace, which we find harmful on MMLU as they did; with neutral text instead, length is free in retrieval. Their masked condition, which we replicate, is the only evidence for pure length effect that remains, and we show that it fails visible control.

sections.title: 3 Setup
sections.content: One principle governs the design: every comparison holds length and evidence position fixed and changes only what surrounds the evidence. We call this the visible-control protocol. It needs forward passes only and applies to any open-weight model. Task. Each context hides one evidence statement, The secret code of the river is 4821., where the key (here, river) is common noun and the value four-digit number. The context ends with the query Question: what is the secret code of the river? Answer: The secret code of the river is, and we score the log-probability ℓ of the correct value under teacher forcing, summed over its tokens. Tokenizers split the value differently (five tokens for Qwen and SmolLM2, three for OLMo and Llama), so we compare losses within models, not across them. The evidence sits at depth drawn uniformly over the context. Conditions. For each trial we build four contexts that share the evidence, the query, and the total length L: 3 Condition Content around the evidence short neutral competing masked nothing random numbers, random words, or one repeated sentence statements in the evidence template, keys drawn uniformly from 51 nouns filler hidden from attention, positions preserved We define the loss of condition as = log (pshort/pc), in nats, where pc = eℓc is the probability of the correct value in condition c. The neutral condition isolates length; the difference between competing and neutral isolates content at fixed length. Because keys are drawn uniformly, some competing statements share the queried key and assign it different value. These conflicts are the strongest competitors the filler contains. Their number nconf grows with length (mean 0.8 at 512 tokens, 3.2 at 2,048, 50.5 at 32,768; none in 42 to 48% of 512-token contexts and in no context of 4,096 tokens or more). We recover nconf for every trial by regenerating its context from the recorded seed, which lets us separate competitors that share the key from those that only share the format. Separately, we insert 0 to 5 explicit distractors that share the format but never the key. Masking. In masked, 2D attention mask removes every filler token from attention for all subsequent queries while position indices keep counting through them, so the evidence stays at its original distance from the query and every competitor becomes invisible. The first tokens of the sequence remain visible, preserving the attention sink [6470]. Models and lengths. We test Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct [7], SmolLM21.7B-Instruct [71], OLMo-2-0425-1B-Instruct [72] and the base Llama-3.2-3B [6], at {512, 1024, 2048} tokens for all models and up to 32,768 tokens within each models context window. All runs use float16 weights and PyTorch SDPA attention, on one Apple workstation (64 GB unified memory) and one RTX 4090 laptop GPU (16 GB). Attention mass on the evidence. For each configuration we select, in the short context, the eight (layer, head) pairs that place the most attention on the evidence tokens [7375]. In every condition, is the attention that these heads send from the final query token to the evidence tokens, summed over evidence tokens and averaged over heads. We do not renormalize to exclude the attention sink. We compare predictors of by the coefficient of determination R2 of univariate least-squares fits on a, log(1/a) and log L. Replication of Du et al. [18]. We reproduce their masked-filler protocol on 1,000 MMLU questions with the base Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, inserting 3,750, 7,500, 15,000 or 30,000 masked tokens between the question and its answer options, following their layout, in which the masked positions separate the evidence from the question. We implement masking by deleting the filler tokens and advancing the position indices by the same amount, which we verified to match explicit attention masking on Llama. We report accuracy with Wilson 95% intervals and paired McNemar tests against the unpadded baseline.

sections.title: 4.1 Length is cheap
sections.content: Visible neutral filler barely moves the target. On Qwen2.5-1.5B, the median loss stays at or below 0.006 nats at every length from 8K to 32K tokens and for all three neutral fillers, and accuracy stays between 0.96 and 1.00  (Table 2)  . Qwen2.5-0.5B, SmolLM2 and Llama-3.2-3B show the same behavior up to 4K tokens. OLMo-2-1B is the exception: it loses 0.57 nats with neutral filler at 2,048 tokens (accuracy 0.91).

sections.title: 4.2 Competition is not
sections.content: Filling the same positions with competing statements instead of neutral text turns free context into failing one. On Qwen2.5-1.5B, the median loss reaches 2.82, 3.94, 4.03 and 4.76 nats at 8K, 16K, 24K and 32K tokens, and accuracy falls to 0.11 to 0.21; on Qwen2.5-0.5B, the loss reaches 1.79 to 4.07 nats and accuracy 0.17 to 0.40. Length is the same in both conditions; only content differs (Figure 1). The loss concentrates on conflicts  (Table 3)  . sections.title: 4.3 One quantity predicts the failure: attention on the evidence

R2(log(1/a)) ranges from 0.35 to 0.58, against 0.02 to 0.08 for log L; bootstrap confidence interval on the difference excludes zero for each model, and the ordering holds within each (length, depth) cell. The relation extends to long contexts: from 8K to 32K tokens, R2(log(1/a)) is 0.32 on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 0.33 on Llama-3.2-3B, against 0.02 and 0.03 for log L; on SmolLM2-1.7B, up to its 8K window, it is 0.45 against 0.18. summarizes the effect of conflicts rather than adding to it: once log(1/a) is known, nconf raises R2 by at most 0.04. sections.title: 4.4 Masking is not a length control
sections.content: Masking reproduces the length-alone effect of Du et al. [18]. On MMLU, accuracy falls with the number of masked tokens on both models, plateauing beyond 15,000 on Llama-3.2-3B (Table 5; all paired McNemar tests against the baseline 0.007). From 7,500 tokens onward, Qwen2.5-7B loses 11.3 to 17.7 points, against 15.5 to 21.1 for Llama-3.1-8B in Du et al. [18, Table 3], so the effect is not specific to one model family. The same intervention degrades retrieval, whereas the filler it hides does not. In Table 2, the masked context loses 1.20 nats and 46 points of accuracy at 32K tokens, while the identical filler left visible loses nothing. Across the three neutral fillers at 32K, accuracy is 0.96 to 0.99 when visible and 0.48 to 0.54 when masked. context of masked tokens at preserved positions is therefore not context of irrelevant tokens: it presents the model with long positional gaps that it never encounters in training [9, 7680], and its cost should not be read as the cost of length. The effect is model-dependent: on Qwen2.5-0.5B, masking costs 0.1 to 0.4 nats. MMLU shows the same ordering at 4,096 tokens on Qwen2.5-1.5B: 59.1% without filler, 57.5% with visible neutral filler, 53.9% with the filler masked. Length is not free in every form, however: visible whitespace padding lowers the same model to 36.0% at 4,096 tokens, an effect absent at 2,048. We have no visible-filler arm on MMLU beyond 4K tokens, so the drops in Table 5 cannot be attributed to the positional gap alone.

sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: Curate, do not truncate. In retrieval, thousands of neutral tokens cost nothing, while few statements that compete with the evidence cost most of the accuracy. The effective budget of context is therefore not its token count but the number of statements that compete for the query. For retrieval-augmented generation [81, 82], agent memory [83] and long-document pipelines, this reverses common priority: deduplicating and resolving conflicting statements before they reach 7 the model [8488] should matter more than shortening the context. Measure attention, not only accuracy. Conflicts, length and depth reach the loss through one measurable quantity: once log(1/a) is known, the number of conflicts adds at most 0.04 to R2. Softmax dilution accounts predict exactly this [62, 63, 89]; we observe it on measured attention, trial by trial. Because requires only forward pass, it can serve as diagnostic for any open model and any retrieval benchmark. The threshold (near 0.35 on Qwen2.5-1.5B, at model-dependent point elsewhere) and slopes above 1 indicate nonlinear readout: the model absorbs moderate loss of evidence mass, then fails abruptly. We predict that methods which sharpen attention at long range [58, 59, 90100] help most when they keep above it. Report visible control. Masking tokens at preserved positions creates long positional gaps absent from pretraining [101103]. In retrieval, this intervention costs 46 accuracy points where the same filler left visible costs none, so its cost is not the cost of length. We recommend that any claim about the effect of length include visible neutral-text control at the same positions. Whitespace padding on MMLU shows that some forms of length do hurt reasoning, so the two accounts are not exclusive: competition dominates retrieval, and length effects remain possible in reasoning.

sections.title: 6 Limitations
sections.content: a is measured in the same forward pass as the loss and we ran no intervention on it, so our evidence is predictive, not causal. The predictor analysis covers 512 to 2,048 tokens on five models and 8K to 32K on two. In our competing filler, the number of conflicts grows with length, and every context of 4,096 tokens or more contains at least one, so the effect of format-only competitors above 2K tokens is not measured; the conflict analysis was not preregistered. is read at single query token, from eight heads, without removing the attention sink. Value tokenization differs across models, so losses are comparable within but not across models. All results come from one synthetic retrieval task and models of at most 3B parameters, except the 7B model in the MMLU replication, which has no visible-filler arm beyond 4K tokens.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: In retrieval, long contexts do not fail because they are long. They fail when what they contain competes with the evidence, and the attention that the evidence keeps tells us when. Context engineering, not context length, is the lever.
